In [[geometry]], the '''gyroelongated pyramids''' (also called ''augmented [[antiprism]]s'') are an infinite set of [[polyhedron|polyhedra]], constructed by adjoining an {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramid]] to an {{nowrap|{{mvar|n}}-gonal}} [[antiprism]].<ref name=rajwade>{{cite book
 | last = Rajwade | first = A. R.
 | title = Convex Polyhedra with Regularity Conditions and Hilbert's Third Problem
 | series = Texts and Readings in Mathematics
 | year = 2001
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=afJdDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA89
 | page = 89
 | publisher = Hindustan Book Agency
 | isbn = 978-93-86279-06-4
 | doi = 10.1007/978-93-86279-06-4
}}</ref>

There are two ''gyroelongated pyramids'' that are [[Johnson solid]]s made from regular triangles, square, and pentagons. A triangular and hexagonal form can be constructed with [[coplanar]] faces. Others can be constructed allowing for [[isosceles triangle]]s.

|-
| [[Image:Gyroelongated pentagonal pyramid.png|100px]] || [[Gyroelongated pentagonal pyramid]] ('''J11''') || 15 triangles, 1 pentagon
|-
||[[File:Augmented_hexagonal_antiprism_flat.png|100px]] || [[Gyroelongated hexagonal pyramid]]<BR>(Coplanar faces) || 18 triangles, 1 hexagon
|}
